title: Fractional Phase Fragmentor — kernel-aware hedged routing and fairness envelopes
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Problem: As our serving surface encounters increasingly diverse request shapes (short interactive chat turns, long prefill-heavy completions, and mixed-length streaming), the current monolithic phase splitter either over-fragments (hurting throughput) or under-fragments (hurting P99 latency). We also have a blind spot: kernel selection hints (quantized vs fp16, fused-attn kernel variants) are not consistently used by the scheduler, so requests with identical phase characteristics are routed suboptimally across GPUs.

Goal: Implement a Fractional Phase Fragmentor (FPF) that: (1) splits prefill/decode work into fractional micro-phases guided by attention-cost heuristics, (2) attaches kernel-affinity hints to fragments and routes using a hedged routing strategy to reduce tail latency, and (3) enforces per-tenant fairness envelopes so throughput-focused jobs cannot starve latency-critical traffic. The feature should reduce P99 latency on mixed workloads by >=20% while keeping token/sec throughput loss <10% for 95% of traffic classes.

Design overview:
- Fractional fragmentation: instead of forcing a single phase boundary for prefill->decode, FPF may split stages into fractional units (e.g., prefill: 0..0.25, 0.25..0.6, 0.6..1.0) based on estimated attention cost and kv-cache size. The splitter uses a lightweight cost model (attention ops estimate + kv cache growth heuristic) to pick breakpoints.
- Kernel-aware hints: each fragment carries a kernelAffinity tag (e.g., "fused-attn-v2", "sparse-attn-probe", "gemm-quant-q4_0"). The scheduler can prefer devices where probe telemetry (last-5-min kernel latency profile) indicates headroom for that kernel.
- Hedged routing: for latency-critical fragments we issue speculative hedged sends to up to N candidate workers (N default 2) and cancel the slowest. Hedging is selective — reserved for fragments where predicted hedged benefit > threshold (based on cost variance history).
- Fairness envelopes: each tenant/request class has an adaptive credit envelope; FPF consumes envelope credit when creating extra hedged work or when fragmenting aggressively. Envelope depletion throttles fragmentation aggressiveness and hedging frequency.
- Fallbacks: if kernel telemetry is stale or candidate pool small, fallback to conservative single-route assignment. If hedged cancellation fails (rare), record metrics and rely on quota reconciliation to avoid double-billing.

Metrics and success criteria:
- Latency: P50/P95/P99 token emit latencies; target P99 improvement >=20% on mixed workloads vs baseline.
- Throughput: normalized tokens/sec under steady-state synthetic workloads; target <10% regression for 95% quantile.
- Resource efficiency: fractional fragmentation should not increase GPU memory usage >5% on average.
- Fairness: measure headroom fairness index (max slowdown caused by higher-priority tenants) and ensure no tenant suffers >30% degradation vs baseline.

Implementation plan:
1) Cost model prototype (2 weeks): implement attention-op estimator and kv-cache growth predictor; offline validation against traces.
2) Fragment format & kernelAffinity (1 week): extend request envelope with fragment metadata and affinity tag.
3) Hedged routing engine (3 weeks): integrate hedging layer into router with selective heuristics and cancellation semantics.
4) Fairness envelope controller (2 weeks): implement per-tenant adaptive crediting, observability counters, and throttling hooks.
5) Canary rollouts & benchmark (3 weeks): compare across representative client mixes, run A/B testing with canary fraction, collect dashboards.
6) Iterate: tune thresholds and cost model parameters, add model-driven auto-tuning.

Trade-offs and alternatives considered:
- Full replication vs hedging: full duplicate execution increases cost too much. Selective hedging offers better tail-latency cost trade-off.
- Static fragmentation rules: simpler but brittle; fractional, heuristic-driven splitting adapts better to mixed workloads.
- Kernel scheduling centralized vs decentralized: centralized decisions can be more optimal but add control-plane latency. We opt for a hybrid: local router uses cached telemetry and falls back to control-plane when necessary.

Risks and mitigations:
- Double resource consumption from hedging: mitigate via tight cancellation windows, envelope credits, and conservative hedging thresholds.
- Regression on throughput-heavy customers: provide per-customer opt-out and conservative defaults; use rollout gates tied to throughput SLIs.
- Complexity of cost model: start with a small set of features and iterate; keep model explainable for debugging.

Rollback plan: disable fractional fragmentation and hedging via runtime flag; automatically revert to current phase splitter and single-route scheduler.
acceptance_criteria: Canary shows >=20% reduction in P99 tail latency on mixed workload benchmark compared to baseline
Token/sec throughput regression <10% for 95% of traffic classes in steady-state tests
No >30% degradation for any tenant in fairness headroom tests
End-to-end e2e canary rollout path and runtime config flag to disable FPF exist
Design doc and bench dashboards linked and reviewed by runtime and infra leads
